content: The United States Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) and the Independent United Kingdom Panel on Breast Cancer Screening have both conducted evidence synthesis reports to evaluate the effectiveness of breast cancer screening. Across all analyses, the I-squared statistic was below 50%, and no significant heterogeneity was observed. The quality of evidence was not downgraded for indirectness, although concerns were raised regarding the age of the trials (which began between 1963 and 1991), the interchangeability of film and digital mammography, and whether the follow-up periods were sufficient to fully assess the benefits of screening. Due to the limited number of trials included, statistical assessment of publication bias was not feasible. The Swedish Two-County Trial was treated as two separate trials (Kopparberg and Östergötland). Modeling data on breast cancer mortality and screening intervals were developed using six independent models from the National Cancer Institute’s Cancer Intervention and Surveillance Modeling Network. These models assumed a cohort of women born in 1960, followed from age 25 throughout their lifetimes. All models used consistent age-specific variables for breast cancer incidence, mammography test characteristics, treatment algorithms, and competing causes of death unrelated to breast cancer. The models consistently ranked screening strategies. Biennial screening retained 81% of the benefits of annual screening while reducing false-positive results by nearly half. Biennial screening reduced breast cancer mortality by 5% compared to no screening. Starting biennial screening at age 40 instead of 50 reduced mortality by an additional 3%, though it required more resources and resulted in more false positives. Extending biennial screening beyond age 69 provided some additional mortality reduction but significantly increased overdiagnosis in older populations. Data from randomized controlled trials on mastectomy rates, with a median follow-up of approximately 11 years, showed that treatment patterns and provider decisions heavily influenced outcomes, making it difficult to attribute changes solely to screening. Evidence on overtreatment was limited and outdated, reflecting changes in treatment practices over time. False-positive rates per screening round were higher in North America compared to European programs, with observational studies showing rates of 98,000 per million women screened for ages 39–49, 92,000 for ages 50–69, and 69,000 for ages 70–74. The evidence on all-cause mortality from randomized trials, with a median follow-up of 11 years, was rated as low quality due to indirectness and outdated trial designs. While confidence intervals included both potential benefits and harms, the large sample sizes and high number of events suggested no imprecision in the estimates. However, the trials’ short follow-up periods and low participation rates limited their applicability to current screening practices. Overall, the findings highlight the trade-offs between the benefits and harms of mammography screening, including reductions in breast cancer mortality, false-positive results, and overdiagnosis. These results were adapted from various systematic reviews, including those conducted by the Canadian Task Force on Preventive Health Care and the Cochrane Collaboration, as well as observational studies and modeling analyses.
